1.title: Network Policies
1.text: Welcome to Module nine: Network Policies. It covers the exam area Services and Networking. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, and every task was run on a real cluster, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do six things. The model in six sentences. Anatomy. The and versus or trap. Common recipes. Reading and debugging. Practice with six hands-on labs worth forty-four points.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: Services and Networking (twenty percent). Practice in this module: six labs, forty-four points, about forty-eight minutes. Exam format: performance-based tasks in a live terminal, scored on the final cluster state. Validated on: Kubernetes version one point thirty-seven point zero with kind net.

1.title: The model in six sentences
1.text: The model in six sentences. By default all Pods accept all traffic (and send all traffic). A Network Policy selects Pods with pod Selector and says which directions it governs in policy Types ( Ingress, Egress, or both). Once any policy selects a Pod for a direction, that direction is default deny for the Pod, and only what the policies allow gets through. Policies are additive: the allowed traffic is the union of all policies that select the Pod. There are no deny rules. Policies are namespaced: a policy protects Pods in its own namespace only. Allowed traffic is described by peers ( from for ingress, to for egress) and ports.

1.title: Common recipes
1.text: Common recipes. Deny all ingress to every Pod in a namespace. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study. Exam tip: When you restrict egress, always allow D N S on port fifty-three, for both U D P and T C P.

1.title: Common recipes, continued
1.text: Common recipes. (no ingress rules at all). Same with Egress to deny all outgoing traffic. Allow all ingress: ingress (one empty rule) with policy Types Ingress. Allow from a namespace: namespace Selector match Labels team frontend. Label the namespace if needed: kube control label ns fe team frontend. Every namespace also has the automatic label Kubernetes dot io slash metadata dot name name, handy when you have no label to use. Restrict egress but keep D N S working. Once egress is restricted, Pods can no longer ask Core D N S, so name lookups fail. Always allow port fifty-three in both protocols.

1.title: Reading and debugging
1.text: Reading and debugging. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study. Exam tip: The default is allow all: the first policy that selects a Pod makes that direction deny by default.

1.title: Reading and debugging, continued
1.text: Reading and debugging. A blocked connection times out (no "connection refused"). Typical bugs: label typos ( role front versus role frontend; Lab nine point four), a selector in the wrong namespace, a missing ports entry, forgetting D N S in an egress policy, or the policy's pod Selector not matching the target Pods. The exam tasks focus on Pod-to-Pod rules; read the task for the namespace and the labels of both sides.

1.title: Lab 9.1: default deny
1.text: Lab nine point one: default deny. This task is worth six points, and you should plan about six minutes. Start by switching to the kind-C K A context. In the namespace np one, the Pod web (engine X) and the Pod client (busy box) can talk to each other. Create a Network Policy named default deny ingress that blocks all incoming traffic to every Pod in the namespace and allows nothing. Outgoing traffic is not restricted. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

1.title: Lab 9.1: default deny, Solution
1.text: Here is one way to solve it. kube control dash n np one apply dash f -. The manifest comes next, as shown on the screen. Then sleep five. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

1.text: Lab nine point two: allow from namespace. This task is worth seven points, and you should plan about eight minutes. Start by switching to the kind-C K A context. In the namespace np two, the Pod api (engine X, port eighty) must accept T C P traffic on port eighty only from Pods in namespaces that carry the label team frontend. Everything else must be denied. The namespace fe has the label team frontend and the namespace other does not. Create one Network Policy named api from frontend in np two. In the namespace np three, the Pod app (busy box) must only be allowed to send traffic to (a) Pods labelled app db on T C P port eighty and (b) the cluster D N S on port fifty-three (U D P and T C P). 2.title: Lab 9.4: fix policy labels
2.text: Lab nine point four: fix policy labels. This task is worth seven points, and you should plan about seven minutes. Start by switching to the kind-C K A context. In the namespace np four, the Pod backend should be reachable on port eighty from the Pod frontend (label role frontend ), but requests fail since a Network Policy was added. Fix the Network Policy backend in (keep its name; do not delete or relabel the Pods) so that frontend can reach backend while the Pod intruder (label role intruder ) still cannot. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

2.title: Lab 9.4: fix policy labels, Solution
2.text: Here is one way to solve it. Run kube control dash n np four get netpol backend in dash o yaml then pipe to grep -A three from. Then kube control dash n np four get pods the show labels flag. Then kube control dash n np four patch netpol backend in the type flag set to json dash p op replace, path slash spec slash ingress slash zero slash from slash zero slash pod Selector, and so on. Then sleep five. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

2.title: Lab 9.6: deny all allow dns
2.text: Lab nine point six: deny all allow dns. This task is worth eight points, and you should plan about nine minutes. Start by switching to the kind-C K A context. 2.title: Recall Check 1
2.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. What is the default network behavior without any policy? Answer: All traffic between Pods is allowed. Question two. What happens to ingress for a Pod once a policy with policy Types Ingress selects it? Answer: Ingress becomes default deny except what the policies allow. Question three. What does an empty pod Selector in spec select? Answer: Every Pod in the policy's namespace.

2.title: Recall Check 2
2.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. Two selectors in the same from item, versus two items: what is the difference? Answer: Same item is and; separate items are or. Question five. How do you allow traffic from another namespace? Answer: With a namespace Selector on that namespace's labels (label the namespace if needed). Question six. Why does an egress policy often break name resolution, and how do you fix it? Answer: It blocks traffic to Core D N S; allow U D P and T C P port fifty-three in an egress rule.

2.title: Recall Check 3
2.text: Recall check three. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question seven. How does a blocked connection look to the client? Answer: It times out. Question eight. Can a Network Policy protect Pods in a different namespace than its own? Answer: No; it governs only Pods in its own namespace.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Default: allow all; first policy makes the selected direction deny-by-default. Spec: pod Selector, policy Types, ingress dot from, egress dot to, ports. Peers: pod Selector, namespace Selector, ip Block. and or or: one dash equals and, separate dashes equals or. Deny all: pod Selector plus policy Types and no rules. Egress: always allow D N S fifty-three (U D P and T C P). Debug: describe netpol, get pods the show labels flag, W get -T three from a client. In the next module, we continue the course.
